LLM Text and Tokens

How source documents are converted into tokens in the LLM transformer model

The model never “sees” words directly. It processes token IDs as vectors, transforms them through attention layers, and predicts the next token. Tokenization converts raw text into a compact, learnable code. Transformers enrich this code with context via attention, then decode it back to text by predicting tokens one by one.

Term Meaning
Token Smallest text unit the model processes (subword/byte/punctuation).
Vocabulary Fixed set of tokens with IDs (e.g., 32k–200k entries).
Embedding Learned vector representing a token/position.
Self‑attention Mechanism computing how strongly tokens relate within the context.
Decoding Strategy to choose next token from probabilities (greedy, top‑k, nucleus, beam).

Tokenization Details

Aspect Summary Example
Subword units (BPE/Unigram) Frequent substrings become tokens; handles rare words, morphology. "unhappiness" → "un", "happiness" or "un", "happy", "ness"
Byte‑fallback Unknown characters split to bytes to ensure coverage of any Unicode text. Emoji or script not in vocab → byte tokens
Special tokens Markers like BOS/CLS, EOS, padding, or role tokens steer model behavior. <BOS>, <EOS>, <PAD>
Chunking / context window Long documents are split into windows; attention is limited to context length. Sliding windows with overlap for retrieval or summarization

From IDs to Contextual Meaning

  • Embeddings: map IDs to dense vectors; similar tokens → similar vectors.
  • Positional info: sinusoidal or learned encodings let the model know order.
  • Self‑attention: tokens weight other tokens to build context‑aware representations.
  • Residual blocks & normalization: stabilize deep learning and preserve gradients.
  • Output head: projects contextual vectors back to vocabulary logits for next‑token prediction.
